utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, except that the first topic this morning, intercepts, is going to be handled by Mr. Josse, Your Honour. But yes, we are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then before I invite Mr. Josse to continue, Mr. Krajisnik, again you're reminded that you're bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before I begin, Your Honour, could I introduce a new member of our team. It's a barrister from Australia sitting two to the left of me Ms. Julie Condon. It also serves as an opportunity to introduce her through the Court to Mr. Krajisnik because of the obvious practical difficulties involved with his giving evidence. He too hasn't met her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Welcome in court. Coming from such a distance, from Australia, but -- you'll stay for a long time or how long will you be on the team? Two months? So we'll have the opportunity to -- have the pleasure to know that the Defence team is assisted by you for this period of time. Thank you. Mr. Josse. Thank you for introducing your new team member and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, on Friday, we handed out a mini bundle of exhibits. I hope everyone, including the interpreters, have brought them from courtroom number 1. I assume they have been brought through. So there is no confusion about this, Mr. Krajisnik, I can see from here, has his own copy of these which I, as I think Your Honour is aware, handed to him via a security officer as soon as the Court had risen. I better just check that Mr. Krajisnik hasn't marked that bundle because otherwise it may be of some concern to my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Mr. Krajisnik, is that bundle marked?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are minor notes that I made in the margin, maybe underlined a few things. You can have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any problem with the markings, I take it if Mr. Krajisnik made his own reminders and observations on it, perhaps then another copy should be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I would be anxious Mr. Krajisnik keep the marked copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are prepared to have it copied in due course, if my learned friends want to check those markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Krajisnik, you can use your own marks but if the document would be tendered as evidence then, of course, we should take a clean copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll provide that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The first exhibit in fact is not there, Mr. Krajisnik. It's the only one that is not there and we are going to refer to it very briefly; puts another one of these intercepts into context. It's P292 KD 30403 which the Court had a number of copies of on Friday. And perhaps that could be put up on the screen. It's tab 42 in our --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The date would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The date is the 2nd of September 1991. It's an intercept between this witness and Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I can help you with this to some extent. This intercept was exhibited through Mr. Kljuic. It was played to the Court on the 28th of September 2004 and Mr. Kljuic said of it that we can use this to explain the power that the SDS had in its propaganda machine by the illegitimate media and that media in Bosnia was all important. And I suspect that he was referring in particular to the name that we see at the top of this intercept, Mr. Nedjo Miljanovic. First of all, who was Miljanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedjo Miljanovic. Actually there are two men with the last name of Miljanovic. This one should be the director of Radio-Television Sarajevo at the time. There is another Miljanovic, however, and maybe from the context I could find out exactly which one this is but I think it's the director of television Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think you're right about that. And this intercept was used, if I can paraphrase what I've already said, by Mr. Kljuic to illustrate the control that your party had over this man and over Sarajevo television. Before I ask you specifically about that subject, perhaps we could all turn to tab 50 in the mini bundle that we've got. This is an intercept between again yourself and Mr. Karadzic on the 18th of September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This, Your Honour, has not been previously exhibited. I don't intends to play it but it does need a number of some sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D180, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the English, on the second page, we see about halfway down the page, it's a third of the way down the page. Dr. Karadzic says and I'll read this slowly: "Look, Momo, we really have to finish that for the television today. People from the television told me that it's a disaster. First of all you saw that rotten television where they made a comment on Kljuic's every word; second of all, all that cynicism and everything; third of all they are kicking Zoric out now." "You say kicking him out?" Karadzic: "From the position of news editor they are offering him to go to advertising and such silly things. Second of all, I mean, it is complete humiliation and we won't -- we will ask and demand that a resignation be handed in and that some sort of parity be established there and that" -- Krajisnik: "Listen to me for a second please. Give Milicevic a call." Karadzic: "He can't do anything. Which Milicevic?" Krajisnik: "Wait a second. No, Miljanovic, what's his name again? Karadzic: "He's a cunt he won't -- Krajisnik: "I know, but to see what's going on to make it but easier for ourselves." Karadzic: "No, I mean there's no use of him, there is no use of him because he's a cunt. Man, he's allowing for not a single Serb to be there. Well, that's" -- . Krajisnik: "Yes, but look at it this way, why wouldn't we take advantage of that? That I don't understand." Is this a reference to the same Mr. Miljanovic, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the reference to the same Miljanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not to put too fine a point on it, why is Dr. Karadzic calling Mr. Miljanovic a cunt in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all because he's vulgar in this conversation, just as I am, and he's calling people bad names. But the underlying thing is that he was a very easily scared man, an apparatchuk a man of the regime from before the elections, when people were getting appointments according to the so-called key of proportionate representation, not because of their competences or on some ethical grounds. Mr. Karadzic at least had that opinion. My opinion was a bit different but the truth lay somewhere in between probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What do you say to Mr. Kljuic's assertion that Miljanovic was someone who was a patsy of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic used the language that was accepted at the time. If somebody was a Muslim he was necessarily a member of the SDA. If somebody was a Croat he belonged to the HDZ and if a Serb then he was SDS. Which wasn't true. Mr. Miljanovic was -- I'm going to try to explain -- director of the television but the editor-in-chief, the programming editor, was a Croat. And they were not allowing a change that would enable parties to place people they wanted appointed instead, appointments were made on a different basis so that people could say, look, you have a Serb there and he's working for the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. Before counsel continues just very briefly there have been two references to Mr. Kljuic's testimony. If possible I would appreciate a citation to the specific page and also, if the witness -- this will be true for forthcoming questions as well, if there is reference to the witness's testimony, if we could know whether it's a direct quotation or a paraphrase that would be helpful as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, first of all the reference is to transcript page 6254 to 6256. And it was a very slight paraphrase on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before we leave this passage, Mr. Krajisnik, I want to ask you about the first part of this extract that I read out which was Dr. Karadzic's part where he said, look, Momo we really have to finish that for the television today. Later on in that same passage he says first of all you saw that rotten television where they made a comment on Kljuic's every word. What's that a reference to and what does he mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned a few days ago that the radio and television and all the other media but radio and television especially was a constant subject of disagreement between the two sides, between the Serb side and the newly formed coalition of Muslims and Croats. In this specific case, the subject of the argument is the programming policy. As I said the programming editor was a Croat, Nenad Pejic, and I think it was Dr. Karadzic who said that in the programming policy, the anchor who was asking questions of Mr. Kljuic did not satisfy himself with getting Mr. Kljuic to present his position but the anchor on top made a commentary of what Mr. Kljuic had said the previous evening in a lopsided and biased way. And Mr. Karadzic was making these comments from the view point of the fact that it was the assembly that charted the programming policy of the radio and television, the television was under the assembly, and they had a problem with the reporting of the television, and he made specific reference to the appearance of Mr. Kljuic on television on the previous night, which was accompanied by such a commentary. That was unacceptable to the Serb side from the viewpoint of their policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on, please, to tab 48, which is the first intercept in the small bundle. This is an intercept between you and Dr. Karadzic on the 9th of September of 1991. It's relatively short and I think I am going to ask Mr. Sladojevic to play it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, si there now agreement? We had some difficulties in the translation, especially with the French channel, that one of the French interpreters will follow the original text and see whether what is said in English is a translation of it and the other interpreter taking time -- and also checking whether the English translation is what he hears at that moment and the other interpreter taking sufficient time to translate so that we have everything on the record. I'm just thinking about technicalities, Mr. Josse, so we have a complete transcript also in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will allow the technicians 30 seconds, Your Honour. If he's unable to fix the problem, I'll deal with it another way. I will, if I may, Your Honour, deal with it another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to read to you a passage about halfway down the first page of this particular intercept, where you begin talking about someone called Zepinic is going there. "I'll call Cengic now and tell him. I see they are taking it very seriously, and here too" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, Mr. Sladojevic has got it to work in which case I haven't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do hear something but it's not loud enough to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am going to leave it, if I could give that instruction that I'm happy to deal with it this other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "I see they are taking it very seriously, and here too. What could that mean but they are only bullies who believe that Bosanska Krupa is managed by those people. Do you understand?" Karadzic: "Yes, yes." Krajisnik: And I see the SDA leaders here really want peace and they feel these -- this big problem turns in the direction those guys want. Do you understand?" Answer: "Yes, yes." Krajisnik: "Which we must admit is possible in any location."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speaker please slow down? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "And probably on our side too there are those who want to be a local political leaders." Karadzic: "It is, but is this -- if this is a comprehensive part of the SDA's policy then we must react." Krajisnik: "It isn't. I could see Mahmutcehajic. That it is not and he said, 'Please, I completely agree and we are against this.' Now, what I'll do I'll see what Cengic says and in that case we'll do it because after all, you know for God's sake, some small village wants to pursue politics." Karadzic: "Yes, yes." Krajisnik: "Of course, it's completely unfounded. It is -- it is wrong, then we'll have to make a war for ourselves." Karadzic: "Yes, yes." Krajisnik: "No way. I can only suppose what that would mean. Do you understand me, you know?" Karadzic: "Yes, yes. Good." Krajisnik: "Look here, I'll see with Cengic and we'll work it out. We can be there at 3, right." My question to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, a small point I don't think it makes any difference but probably useful to note that there are some small distinctions I noted, I'm sure it happens when people read, between what Mr. Josse read out and the actual language of the translation. None that I saw that were particularly significant. The most distinctive of which occurred when he said, "Of course, it's completely unfounded it is, it is wrong," and then Mr. Josse read out, "Then we'll have to make a war for ourselves." The transcript itself says, "Then we'll have made a war for ourselves." Again, I don't think any of those were particularly significant. It may have been hard for him to not that, though, so I -- I put that on the record in case it becomes for some reason significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're working for from a different copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not? Just misread?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Misread. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, my question about this passage is, what is this all about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is about an incident that happened in Bosanska Krupa. This Court has heard the interpretation of an intercept between Mr. Vjestica and Dr. Karadzic concerning the destruction of the monument to Branko Copic, a Serb poet. He is a Serb but he is somewhat of an institution for the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was a witness from Krupa who spoke about this here. I think he was president of the municipal assembly, who was explaining why that monument should not have been in the park but in another location. That's the incident concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what stance are you taking in the course of your conversation with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, just one thing, Mr. Karadzic was upset because he had received information directly from Krupa, from Serb representatives, whereas I heard the same report and I tried to sort of dissipate the tension, and I was telling Karadzic, think of the Croats and Muslims. We will have a war if we react to every little thing somebody does on the ground because I had the impression that Muslim representatives on the republic level had a position not unlike mine. They condemned what happened in Krupa, and I thought we should try to play that down and avoid a war, rather than react to every incident. I thought we should clear things up and try to redress the situation. And that can be understood from the rest of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And who was excuse me pronunciation, Mr. Mahmutcehajic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mahmutcehajic was either one of the Deputy Prime Ministers in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina on behalf of the SDA. I think he was deputy minister for science or something like that. Dr. Mahmutcehajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rusmir was his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You say, look here, I'll see with Cengic and we'll work it out. Why did you say that and what made you feel that you could work it out with Mr. Cengic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic was also Deputy Prime Minister, also on behalf of the SDA, and he held a very high position in the SDA. This was state business, not party business, and Mr. Cengic had shown goodwill. So I thought I would call him up and try to deal with this situation because I knew that he was well intentioned, and Serbs had a lot of sympathy for him. Even when he spoke out against us, we didn't hold it against him. We thought he was sincere and a man of goodwill, and I thought he would sincerely try to help and redress the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to go to the next -- that needs a number, Your Honour, the one that I have just read out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we could go to the next intercept in the bundle and perhaps that could have a number. That's tab 49, the 10th of September.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's the same two protagonists, Your Honour. I don't wish that to be played. I want to turn to the second page in the English. There is a longish response towards the top of that page from Mr. Krajisnik which I'm going to read out. Mr. Krajisnik says, "'Why did you schedule it?' And he said he told him, help me, tell me what his name is. That's Izetbegovic. So, he said 'he told me,' he said. So I said, so why did you schedule it, I said. 'But I couldn't,' he says, 'wait any more.' I went down there, then I said gallantly like this, 'Do you know what? Please, let no one ever dream of scheduling a session again. It happened now but never again, you know, without me.' And then I said, 'Do you know what? We simply have to sit down tomorrow. This is a specific republic. It's different from others. We have to say clearly that we have different options, that we have differences, that we are a team, that we must solve problems peacefully, et cetera.'" . It may be, Mr. Krajisnik, that you'll need to look at the exchange between you and Mr. Karadzic immediately above the passage that I have just read out, but who are you referring to in the course of that conversation that you were repeating to Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am recounting the conversation between late Professor Abdulah Konjicija and myself. He was president of the citizens council on behalf of the SDA. And going beyond his powers, he convened a session of the assembly or rather started a session of the assembly without my approval and when I arrived I found complete chaos there because women had entered the parliament and it was a very unpleasant scene. They came in to protest the mobilisation of conscripts. I asked if it was Mr. Maksimovic who convened the session. They told me no. They said Konjicija did it, and I asked him why. And his reply was, Izetbegovic told me to. So I said we have a session on the 11th. That session was indeed held. And that's where we are going to discuss all our differences. And we did. On the 11th of September, let me remind this Court, we endorsed a conclusion proposed by Mr. Izetbegovic so the effect that nobody was going to impose any solutions on anybody else. We had different visions of the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina and we were going to arrive at a peaceful solution, a mutually agreed one. And this irregularly convened session was a rather unpleasant event and I didn't want it to sour the atmosphere on the eve of the regular session scheduled for the next day. I have the minutes from that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Later on, in the same intercept, two pages on in the English, you say, "And then say everything that is not good about the second item in carefully chosen words." Karadzic: "Yes, yes." Krajisnik: "One can't dwell on it. One shouldn't get hysterical about it, you know." Again, Mr. Krajisnik, it may be that you want to look at the exchange immediately above the passage that I have just read out but what are you saying that one needs to use carefully chosen words about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be quite honest. I haven't found the text. And the interpreters didn't manage to find it either. But I can give you an answer just off the cuff but I wish I could read it. Could you just assist me with the actual passage? Where is it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think in English we find it on page 4, and the upper part, but in the B/C/S version I have not yet located it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been assisted by the interpreter. 8690 are the last digits on that page. Sorry, maybe I -- maybe you need to find it yourselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We found it in English at upper part of page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This follows the sequence of what I said a few minutes ago. I'm saying, "No, no, no, listen, I don't know who's interest it is whether it should or should not be set on fire." I'm trying to say that it was not in my interest that we have any tensions on the 10th of September if we are going to have an assembly meeting on the 11th of September where one of the most important points should be debated, and that is our differences. Of course, there are other points there as well. Objections made vis-a-vis the foreign minister and then the Martic case and so on and that's why I'm saying one shouldn't get hysterical about it, you know, and things like that. We had meetings of clubs of the presidents of clubs, Mr. Izetbegovic was there too. I think that others were there as well. I can't really remember exactly who it was, and we came to the conclusion that on the 11th we should come up with a conclusion that would be pacifying for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and indeed we did, at the proposal of Mr. Izetbegovic. So that was the effort I made on that day on account of Bosanska Krupa to try to pacify the situation and not to create any further commotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to go to the next intercept in the bundle. That's our reference tab 62, between you and Dr. Karadzic dated the 4th of October 1991. I'm told it's not possible to play this at the moment so again I'll read out --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can check to see if that's available on Sanction in our database. We mentioned earlier to the Defence that might be possible so we are looking now and if Mr. Josse can wait a moment, we'll give him an answer. Apparently that can be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would like it to be played --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll take that option, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll play the whole of it or just a portion?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. The whole of it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Serbs always make mistakes, what? They always call when they don't have and they don't call when they should. All right, what's up? Everything's fine. We've just arrived. When did you arrive? I arrived just now and heard on the radio that they want some meeting and so is there a meeting tonight? I was at the meeting there, you know, uh-huh, but maybe this shouldn't -- maybe we should meet but I don't know when, connected with this Trebinje business and the rest. Uh-huh. Is that for tonight or for tomorrow? Well it's not, we can do it tomorrow. Well, what did they want? It's all under the JNA command. There is no need. What about Trebinje? It doesn't matter. Please, it doesn't matter to me when we'll talk to him. Yes, yes. I think that it can -- I called. I could not find. I, stammering, dictated a statement yesterday which he should -- well, I think you should see what it's about. Obviously, obviously everything should be all right, you know. Yes. They -- they are using it. I told him I dictated the statement and they dictated it to him but I don't know whether he's made it public. See here, Radovan, yes, I spoke this evening, everything regarding peace, unity, everything is fine. It can't be paramilitary. It must be -- no, under no circumstances, well, yes, we don't uphold that. No, under no circumstances, we have and I have told Biljana to say that we do not uphold the idea at all of civilian authorities dealing with military matters. No, I have -- except to, except to help the JNA. Yes, yes, what I want to say is I think that tonight I got a very good impression, you know. Really? At that meeting I don't think there is a single thing we'll do which will be against Bosnia, unity, or peace, and so on. No, no, of course, not. Today I hit on Bogicevic a bit. Really? I made a statement to Vecernje Novosti and the former Politika. Uh-huh. I said all principled he can't establish that it was just a suggestion. Not even the Presidency has the right up there in the assembly. Yes. I mean go away, go fuck your mother, who are you sucking up to? It's easy for you, spread that around. Achieved good and I think that it's in any case all that should be regular under some kind of order and all and not have someone waging a private paramilitary war. It's under no circumstances, no, I only think that our people rush in but it's all under the command of the JNA. It's -- I want to tell you, please, you're tired now and I've just arrived, if I'd known that he would come earlier I would have dropped by. I've just come at this very minute. Yes, really. Yes, yes. Well, about that I must do it right, set it straight. Yes. I even thought of holding a meeting tonight. I told them something. Please, we will never support anything which might ignite the situation in Bosnia. At this moment, we, what happened down there, the army, that's one thing, and we are something else, you know. Yes, yes. I mean, I know we are on the same wave length and he said oh, come on, in fact, they, other important things, and that they see to what extent we are ready for it and to what extent we are not, yes, yes. I said we don't want to do anything rash without checking, attack someone now and I don't know what else. Yes, yes. But want to see if it's all -- what it's all about and whatever is right do it properly. Agreed. I think you know that I know as it was said and we, he and I, sat for a while last night and he was at a meeting, Alija was on television, and that's where we were. Uh-huh, all right. But it is all right. I saw that they all want peace. Well, yes. All right, but what of Stipe? Does Stipe want peace? I'll tell you that when we see each other tomorrow. Agreed. Look here, when you get a good rest, we'll be in touch and meet somehow to work it out. Agreed. It's Saturday but we'll meet, if you want. Yes. We have time. I'll drop by the house. But -- agreed. This thing today for me was very -- I saw it very positively. Excellent. How was it up there? Good, good. Basically good. I see that those results in The Hague are excellent. I'm really satisfied. Excellent, excellent. Excellent, excellent. Many other things are moving in that direction. There are conditions to stop the blood shed and establish peace but now it all depends. The one who doesn't want that will be fucked. Well, yes. The one who doesn't want that will be fucked. There can be no more. The whole world know that is whoever stirs up trouble is finished. That's when what I said when we were at the meeting this evening. Please, just so that you know, that's our stand. Don't accidentally but there is nothing what we say now, Momo speaks to Njegos in the room to pick up the other line. We won't attack any of our people for that, for publicity. We must check to see what it's about. Everything must be according to the rules. We won't budge from any of our stands. Yes, yes, yes. It's different when it's hearsay but what has now happened down here, there is, for sure, while we investigate it, look into it, we'll give it all. Good agreed, agreed. Good. See you tomorrow. Agreed. Okay. Go get some rest. You must be tired. Okay." [as read].

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There are some minor corrections to the existing translation if you want them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sure we do, Madam Interpreter, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is one point approximately one page down where there is a reference to the former Politika. It's not former Politika. It's a newspaper called Politika Ekspres or Ekspres Politika. We'll try to give you the exact page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's at the top of page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's the beginning of page 2. Then three lines down, there is -- just a second. "All that should be regular." It should read, "All that should be by the book." And at the very end, where there is reference to "don't accidentally." That should be "don't even think about or don't even think about it." That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, fairly near the beginning of this conversation, you say, "It can't be paramilitary." What are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, and I think that my memory serves me well -- well, first of all, let me give an answer to your question. I think that our policy, that is to say the Serb policy, has to be that paramilitaries should not be tolerated and cannot be tolerated. That's an answer to your question. If you need a further explanation of that, I'm prepared to provide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think you should put it into the context of this particular conversation and the events of October 1991. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first incident or one of the first incidents in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where the damaged party so to speak were the Croats, that is the village of Ravno near Trebinje, as far as I know, as far as I managed to find out, a group of citizens of Croat ethnicity stopped the army, the army gave an ultimatum and there were even casualties, fatalities there, and so on. We had a meeting then, we the top people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say the Presidency and the president of the assembly and the Prime Minister, I don't know who else -- well, that's what it probably was. So party and state influences were intertwined there. Mr. Kljuic and Mr. Izetbegovic and others also represented their parties. The accusation was that some paramilitary units under civilian authority participated in that incident. I am saying this in connection with Ravno. Now, I am conveying what I said there, and what our position was. They were levelling accusations. Mr. Kljuic was accusing the president of the municipal assembly in Trebinje, Vucurevic, that he had a unit that did that and so on. And then I said here, "Our position is certainly that we are against paramilitary formations, we are going to investigate the matter, and if we establish that that's the way it was, everyone should be punished because we don't want to do anything that would contribute to harming the peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina." I was pleased that Mr. Karadzic confirmed all of that and we were supposed to have a meeting which would certainly be attended by Mr. Karadzic as president of the party. It should have been a different kind of meeting so that we would have a more detailed discussion about this. I managed to convey the atmosphere of this meeting here. It was encouraging. All said that peace was in our interest and that it would be a good thing to resolve such conflicts as soon as they crop up. Not once they take an undesired course, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other thing on this that might help. At the bottom of page 2 in the English, there is a reference to someone called Stipe. That was a Mr. Mesic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Maybe Mr. Karadzic said this because -- well, Stjepan, you know, Stjepan Kljuic is also Stipe for short and he was also perhaps referring to Stipe Mesic. At that time I knew who it was that he meant but now I can't be sure. If -- well, I mean, he could have meant either one of the two. I believe that perhaps, I'm saying perhaps, he meant Kljuic here. Maybe he was using a nickname here in the case of Mr. Kljuic, because the nickname for Stjepan is Stipe. Maybe he did mean Stjepan Mesic too but I'm not sure, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Either way it was a reference to a Croatian leader; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He certainly meant the Croatian side, perhaps I should put it that way, if that is an explanation. He meant the Croatian side, whether it's at the level of Bosnia or at the level of Croatia or Yugoslavia. I think at that time Mr. Stjepan Mesic was the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia. I think he still was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I asked for a number for that. I don't think I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Don't think you did. Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D183, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like to go to tab 66. I have to apologise to the Court. This has previously been exhibited as part of P292. I don't have the precise number, and will need some assistance as far as that's concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you proceed while the OTP is trying to assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My apologies. In fact, it's only a small part of this that I wish to ask you about, Mr. Krajisnik. It was adduced during the evidence of Mr. Babic. I think Mr. Tieger can help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can't unless I have the date. We don't have the tab numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 16th of October of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Krajisnik, Karadzic, and Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. And as I've already said, it was adduced. I don't even know, I'm afraid, whether it was played but it was adduced during the evidence of Mr. Kljuic. I beg your pardon, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to read a passage of this very slowly so the interpreters can find the right part. It's at the very bottom of the second page in the English where it talks about 1200 hours. And Mr. Koljevic says, "Well, tomorrow, early in the morning, we can do today in the afternoon any way." Karadzic: "Today in the afternoon, I have to go." Koljevic: "Okay. Okay. Fine." Karadzic: "I have to do something else tomorrow morning." Koljevic: "You have to even a second meeting." Karadzic: "Yes." Koljevic: "Well, I can arrive in the morning at 700 hours at the conference. It is all the same for me. We are losing ourselves in detail." Karadzic: "Fine, fine, fine." Koljevic: "Please, there is also another reason for which I have -- for which I would have to -- you would have to mention that you -- there were questions last night regarding that sentence." Karadzic: "I will quote Filipovic." Koljevic: "Quote him, well, nothing else, I quoted him." Karadzic: "Yes, yes." What is this a reference to, please, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are saying that Mr. Karadzic should go to a press conference. The most important thing here are the last lines that you read out, when Mr. Koljevic suggests to Mr. Karadzic that he should certainly explain that sentence, and the sentence, if you remember, was referred to several times here. That Karadzic threatened that Muslims would disappear. Karadzic is saying here, "I am just going to quote Mr. Filipovic." Actually, I have evidence here from this press conference where he said at this press conference, what I said is the same thing that Mr. Filipovic said from this rostrum. If we do not reach agreement we are going to disappear as a people. That is the meaning of this explanation, why Mr. Karadzic takes into account this statement which is much longer than what has been interpreted here and has a completely different connotation, that is the reason why Mr. Karadzic presented this at the assembly. He explained it at the press conference and Mr. Koljevic here is telling him that it caused anxiety among the public and that he should explain it at a press conference. There is a newspaper article pertaining to that press conference where you can see that Karadzic explained this. If necessary, it can be presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have it in my archives. I can present it to the Trial Chamber if necessary. Perhaps I even have it here right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, if you're interested to hear and see it, we could invite Mr. Krajisnik to present it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you've got it here now, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I underlined it here. There are two copies. Mr. Josse can get one and you can too. The underlined section is the one that you can perhaps place on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that there are two copies. Perhaps we could put that on the ELMO, have it read so that it then becomes part of the record. It seems to be a -- from -- taken from Politika at the 17th of October 1991. Could it be put on the ELMO, Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, while that's happening I should indicate that that intercept was previously exhibited as P292, KID 30656.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's then on the record as well. Could we then just look on what's on the ELMO at this moment? Don't see anything on our screens. Is there any problem to reproduce what's on the ELMO? I'm looking at the technicians. No, that's not on the ELMO at this moment. Could someone explain to me -- could the technicians explain to me what's the problem to have the ELMO reproduced at this moment? Yes, there we are. Yes. Madam Usher, perhaps we first go to the top of that page to identify what exactly it is. Yes. I see that it's taken from Politika, 17th of October 1991. Mr. Krajisnik, the underlined portion, is that the one in yellow on the right-hand side or is it further down to the bottom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both. But first the lower part should be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I make a suggestion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So could we zoom in so that at least Mr. Krajisnik is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. I take it that you start where it reads, "Radovan --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was ascribed to Radovan Karadzic that he said something about the victimisation of the Muslim people. If you want, I can continue reading this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you read all the yellow highlighted portion, then we could then move to the second part you wanted to draw our attention to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Then this is a quotation, "I quoted Mr. Muhamed Filipovic who at the same rostrum said, if" -- could you please move it to the other part now? "If we do not reach agreement but if some other options are chosen [a forceful division of Bosnia] then that is the beginning of the end of the Muslim people. That, added Karadzic, does not have to be the beginning of the end of his people only in a physical sense but also in the sense that the existence of the national being of the Muslims. I said with the best of intentions that Karadzic once again highlighted what Mr. Filipovic had said." Dr. Karadzic put forth a request that all parties state their views on the fact that the meeting was illegal. That is what I wish to indicate here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, could that have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D184, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then someone has to give at least one copy, preferably a clean copy, I saw Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a clear copy on a CD. I can bring it tomorrow. Both of the ones I have here today are marked but I can get a clear copy from the CD and I also have the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's just see what you would like, Mr. Josse, I wouldn't mind, I mean, marking here means the portions read so therefore it doesn't disturb me that much. But the Prosecution? No problem. So we could work on the basis of this copy so if one of them could be then tendered and be given to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does the Chamber wish to have the whole article translated by the CLSS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would -- as a matter of fact I would rather delay the decision until the Prosecution has had an opportunity to read the remainder of it and have it perhaps by language assistant explained to it and then see whether they insist on having it translated so if one copy could be given to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps the other copy could be given to my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then Mr. Krajisnik said he still had the original and a copy so then we could work on the basis of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could they just return the annex to me that one -- the one that goes with it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was another document attached to it and that will be separated and the other part will be returned to you, Mr. Krajisnik. Madam Usher, yes, this is one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can move on while --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One copy goes to -- Madam Usher, the other copy goes to the Prosecution and then what remains in the hands of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could Mr. Tieger's microphone be adjusted because the interpreters have trouble hearing him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He immediately followed you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was a welcome introduction by the interpreter. If my learned friend is going on to a different matter I just have one point on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am moving on to a different interpret. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Simply to not that, as before, there were some minor discrepancies between what was actually read out and what appears in the text. Again I don't anticipate it will create a problem but in case someone was relying on the transcript rather than the document itself, the most notable -- nevertheless small -- discrepancy was found at the top of page 3 of the English, where Dr. Koljevic -- Professor Koljevic is speaking. The text of the intercept reads, "Please there is also another reason for which you to have to -- you would have to mention that," and it was read out as "for which I would have to -- I would have to mention."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, that's how it reads in English. For me. "Which I would have to." That's fourth line of page 3 of the English, it reads, "I." Could we have perhaps then that there are two different versions again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Apparently so. I am relying on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at the last three, the -- it is English translation, 02079164, up until 9167, in my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mine too. That's quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's surprising. I wonder whether same documents would have different -- could I have a look at it, at your version, Mr. Tieger, so that I can check what -- because usually there are different versions, whereas -- yes. There seem to be under the same number, different versions, which -- I mean, different numbers different versions is something we have seen before, but here, although it's a minor -- no, perhaps this is not a minor matter but both the layout and in this respect we see that there are different versions. I'd like to -- the Registrar to find out what is the one that is in evidence so that at least we know on which one to focus. It worries me. It really worries me that even under the same number, different versions appear. Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I'm going to say I suspect isn't very helpful but as I observed the other day, Mr. Stewart and I are finding this really all the time, Your Honour, particularly as we've been working on our client's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, under the same number as well. I mean different versions are, I would say, a -- well known; two translations sometimes be made of the same document, but here we find differences within same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd be lying if I was able to verify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what is mainly worrying me. Mr. Tieger, the Chamber very much would like to -- you to find out what caused this to happen and perhaps to make a full comparison because -- to see whether the electronic version is the one or the other, and because this is really worrying us more than any identifiable, different versions, because here, it's almost impossible to detect this, but you yourself were the one who detected it. Mr. Josse, would it be agreeable for you that once Mr. Tieger has done this job and when you have been able to look at P292 KID 30656 to see whether we need a new number for this alternative version of the same document? Josse I'm more than happy to liaise with my learned friend who I am sure will guide me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll hear from you soon. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One last intercept in this batch, please, Mr. Krajisnik. It's the last one in the bundle, which is 115.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this hasn't previously been exhibited. In fact, I'm only going to refer to a very short part of it but it does need a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you and if I may add to the previous one, what seems to be in evidence is not your version but seems to be Mr. Tieger's version. So the request is now to both parties to find out why you're using a different one although the other one seems to have been admitted into evidence and what could cause these different versions to exist. Could it be that these are text documents rather than image documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be hesitant to speculate about any of that at this point but certainly we will do our best to get to the bottom of it. With respect to D185, if we could have the date, please? I presume that's December.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 21st of December, 1991. Your Honour will see in fact in the bundle there are two intercepts for that date. One is 114 which I'm not going to deal with now. And the other is 115. As the Chamber is aware, on that day an assembly session took place; Mr. Stewart is going to deal with that assembly session very shortly. But this intercept, Mr. Krajisnik, really relates to a discrete point. About halfway down the page in the English, and about two-thirds of the way down the first page in the B/C/S, we see that Mr. Koljevic is addressing you and says, "So am I -- I'm also very satisfied, Momo. I've just spoken to Radovan." What form of address did Mr. Koljevic generally use when he was speaking to you, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Koljevic and I were on last name terms, but still we called each other Momo and Nikola. Otherwise, we called each other Professor and president but sometimes in jest we called teach other Momo and Nikola although we were usually on second name terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when he called you "president," was that a reflection on your power in any real sense?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever he told me "president" or "speaker," I knew he was going to tease me. It was that jocular tone he used sometimes. It was far from a relationship of superiority or inferiority in terms of power. It couldn't have meant that. Mr. Koljevic actually occupied a higher position than I so that's completely out of the question. I mean in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well that's a subject which either Mr. Stewart or I will return to a little later on in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes the questions I've got to ask about these intercepts. Mr. Stewart tells me he is happy to proceed. This may be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, I'm looking at the clock and perhaps it's a good moment to have a break as well. We will adjourn until five minutes to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Stewart, there seems to be a rather practical matter I would like to deal with very briefly. Mr. Krajisnik, I -- the Chamber was informed that you received by now the DVDs of your testimony, but that there is one -- and that it also that you are able to review it on your computer. At the same time, there seems still to be a question about the 25th of April. You started your testimony only not at the very beginning of that day but at a later stage. I do understand that you've been provided with a DVD of your testimony, so on from that moment, from the 25th of April, but that you would like to have the remainder of the day on DVD as well? That takes quite some effort to digitalise the whole of the session so therefore I'm just inquiring into where the ruling was that you would receive DVDs of your testimony and not of the whole of the procedure, whether it would assist you if you received the audio of the remainder of that day instead of the -- if that would help, that would certainly alleviate the burden on the shoulders of our technicians. If that would do, then you have it at least available but only in audio. Is that -- would that resolve your problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really appreciate it, Your Honour. But I would really be grateful if they could give me that first part as a video, never mind when. That would be very useful to me. I only have footage from the moment when I started to testify. But I don't have the passage while I was still sitting over there and was unable to write. So I would really like to have that on video even if I have to wait. However, if it's not possible ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter, and it might take some more time. I'm not promising you anything but the audio you could receive very quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, we are going now to the session of the Serb assembly held on the 21st of December. It's the fourth session. The exhibit number of that, Your Honour, is -- the B/C/S is P64(A) so it's Mr. Treanor's stuff, at tab 543, which is found in binder 19. And if he hasn't already got it, Your Honour, Mr. Krajisnik, in the usual way, needs to have the margin-numbered copy of this particular document. It's on its way to him right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if you could go, please, to margin number 1 which is at the very top of page 3, it's also at the very -- well, pretty much at the very top of page 3 of the English at the moment, Your Honours. And we got Mr. Ostojic speaking. Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The second paragraph, just a light introduction, and then he says, "I would like to thank Novi Sad television and Belgrade television for making it possible for the Serbian people in Yugoslavia to watch this session. It means that this session is being broadcast live to the Serbian people in Serbia and Montenegro and in Serbian Krajina as well as to other citizens. I appeal to Sarajevo television to join in with Novi Sad television so that the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina can watch this session, although Sarajevo television has ignored the plea from the president of the simply of the Serbian people, nevertheless I ask you to support this call. We expect Sarajevo television to tune in to the broadcast by Serbian television so that Serbian people in BiH can watch this session." Mr. Krajisnik, had you, as president of the assembly, had you made any representations in relation to television coverage of this particular session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's evident from this that I did, although I can't recall it at the moment. I did appeal on the Sarajevo television to broadcast it, but I can only trust the minutes at this time because I don't have a memory of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Anyway, you personally supported as wide publicity as possible for the assembly session, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is yes, but it's also because I wanted others to be informed about what the Assembly of the Serbian People was doing to avoid any ambiguity and any speculation. It had a double purpose, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say others, you mean -- you mean non-Serbs, do you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not nice to call them non-Serbs, it doesn't sound good. But I really meant all the citizens of the then Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the others, not only Serbs. It doesn't sound so good when you call them non-Serbs or Muslims or this or that. It grates on my ears a bit when you say non-Serbs. I meant all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina rather than Serbs only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, I will have to attach a general apology to any use of that phrase because it's not intended pejoratively by me, of course, but sometimes it's going to be necessary for purely descriptive purposes. Otherwise it gets very convoluted. Mr. Krajisnik, if we can go we can skip number 2 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to really object to the use of that term. I'm just saying that it sounds a bit awkward to our ears, to people over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. I took no offence. The -- nor meant any. Let's skip number 2 and go to margin note number 3, which in the Serbian is on page 7, about the middle of page 7, and in the English is page 5, and it's quite a way into a contribution by Mr. Buha. Mr. Krajisnik, before we look at what Mr. Buha says here, I wonder if -- well, please, could you describe what Mr. Buha's role and level of activity was in the politics as at 21st December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Buha was a deputy, a MP, only that. I'm not aware that he was a member of some body within the party. He was a very renowned professor at the university and he was a very renowned MP, consequently. It had -- his words had more weight than those of another MP as a consequence. I am sure that he wasn't a member of the ministerial council because the ministerial council comprised only ministers, and he wasn't one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, he on this -- in this contribution here, a few paragraphs down, he says, it's a couple of paragraphs down from the letter 3, "At this truly historical moment," you see that? I should read the previous paragraph; it doesn't make so much sense. "Today it is essential" -- against the number 3, the paragraph "today it is essential for the very survival of the Serbian nation ..." Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "... and its cultural, economic and civil prosperity, although it is well known what the Serbian people in BiH and the Serbian people in general stand for in historical, national, and constitutional sense, its reputation in the eyes of European bullies does not seem to be very high at the moment. We suspect that it will not be too long before the criteria for measuring its value and strength that are now being used secretly start being used openly." And just to put this in context, it -- this assembly meeting was taking place in circumstances where the European Community had given the strongest indication to the -- to Bosnia and Herzegovina that it was inviting proposals with a view to independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have that document here as well. It was published in the newspapers. On the 15th of December the European Community sent a query to all the former republics of Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, to let them know whether they wished to become independent states, and if so, to make their applications. So this was said in light of that query by the European Community and the reply sent by our government. And I can elaborate on that if that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, it's -- the -- for present purposes, the simple position was this, wasn't it, that that -- that invitation from the European Community was receiving from the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina a response indicating clearly that, yes, they did wish to move towards independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina? That's the correct summary of the position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With the proviso. Both the Presidency before the Serb representatives and the government, without the Serb representatives, had made a decision to respond to that invitation by saying that, yes, Bosnia and Herzegovina wanted independence, and it was going to apply to the European Community for recognition. And it was concerning these two decisions that were made without a consensus that this session was held, and the immediate reason for convening the session was that invitation of the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So then, Mr. Buha continues, "At this truly historical moment the Muslim and Croatian people ought to, for their part, answer to these questions. For if they have decided that it is in their national interest to leave Yugoslavia, the Serbian people will not be opposed to any lawful move that would lead to the realisation of that interest. The only condition is that they accept the decision of the Serbian people to keep its territory within the remains of Yugoslavia. I suggest that the assembly adopt a constitutional document in this respect. The Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina should demand that the right to remain within Yugoslavia is realised through the institutions at the republican and federal level on the basis of an agreement on succession and the acceptance of international arbitration. The fact remains that the representatives of the Serbian people in the assembly of BiH have constantly insisted that the Croatian people in BiH are constituent. Sadly, it did not instigate a single word from the representatives of the Croatian people in the same house on the analogous status of the Serbian people in Croatia, although it would have been well founded. In the same way that the Croatian ethnic community is autoktonis [phoen] and sovereign on its ethnic and historical territories in BiH, so is the Serbian ethnic community on its ethnic and historical territories in Croatia, even in terms of their populations, despite the horrendous genocide against the Serbs during the NDH, Independent State of Croatia. These two communities are almost of equal size which means that even that condition for equal treatment exists." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, I want to concentrate on that phrase, "ethnic and historical territories," and then look at the next paragraph, "Naturally, we cannot insist on what is self-evident but we can demand that the process of territorial division should be based on ethnic, historical, and territorial principles as well as a clause that the number of the members of the people erecting the border who are left behind the border should be as few as possible and in that respect there should be a balance." Mr. Krajisnik, the phrase "ethnic and historical territories," did it allow a clear and specific definition or was it a more fluid term?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, a specific area was concerned, the area of Krajina. You know that a part of what used to be called military Krajina was in Croatia, whereas another part containing the majority of Serbs was in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The ethnic Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that area had been brought by the Ottomans to defend the border against Croatia whereas on the other side of the border, the ethnic Serbs there had been brought by the Austro-Hungarian empire to defend the border against the Turks. And it is said in a book that that area was always under the control of Vienna, not Zagreb, and it was referred to as a historically ethnic area, when we speak of Serbs in Krajina. Of course, on the other bank of the Una River, the Bosnian Krajina is also an ethnic area but it has a different political dimension. Ottomans had brought Turks from Anatolia, to the Cazin Krajina and they formed the basis of the Muslim population there but those are the historical facts. When Mr. Buha speaks of historical entitlement, before the multi-party elections, Serbs used to be a constituent people along with the Croats, and with the arrival into power of the new government, Serbs were deprived of that status, and that's what Mr. Buha was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Buha, what you have said, Mr. Krajisnik, about the ability to identify or define those territories in that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that part of Croatia, did that apply more generally in Bosnia and Herzegovina to ethnic and historical territories?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There existed certain historical and ethnic territories with a majority Serb, Croat and Muslim populations respectively. I can show you that on the map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I can point out the exact regions where Croats were historically a majority, where Serbs were historically a majority, and where Muslims were historically a majority. And there were again other areas in which no community had a majority. But it was impossible to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina in clearly divided ethnic areas, areas where one ethnic community would be a clear majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Simovic? We see him, if you find point 6, we can go on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, would you allow me to ask one clarifying question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, but of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in the beginning of the speech of Professor Buha, in the B/C/S, it's on page 4, the semi-last paragraph, he says, "Despite a unanimous decision of the assembly of BiH from 16th of October 1991, that no constituent people would be pressurised into accepting the will of the other two, our partners could not live up to their commitment even for a month." Now, earlier today, your testimony, was, "On the 11th of September, let me remind this Court, we endorsed a conclusion proposed by Mr. Izetbegovic so to the effect that nobody was going to impose any solutions on anybody else." Do you consider this a mistake by Professor Buha? Because what you described to have happened on the 11th of September very much resembles what Mr. Buha here describes as what happened on the 16th of October and from what we know of the 16th of October, it was quite a different matter than what he describes here. Do you consider there to be a mistake or -- so we should understand that as a reference to the 11th of September? And then "not even a month" means already in October they violated this commonly adopted decision? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, it is a mistake. On the 11th of September, a meeting of the assembly was held and we have a document here where conclusions were adopted on the basis of Mr. Izetbegovic's proposals. Mr. Buha made a mistake here. It's illogical because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought when I tried to verify it with you. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we were going to look just above marginal note 6 on your copy, Mr. Krajisnik, so that will be -- in fact it's on page 16 of the -- of your version, and it's on page 9 of the English, in each case towards the top of the page we see Mr. Simovic starting to talk and his -- it was -- was he -- just a deputy but was he a deputy only or did he have some other role or function?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Miodrag Simovic was not a deputy. He was Deputy Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who had been nominated by the Serbian democratic party. You see that he was saying here what had happened at the government meeting in connection with the letter sent by the European Community. Since he is speaking before the assembly, that creates a bit of confusion, as if he were a MP, but no, he is actually Deputy Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I don't know whether he was here at the same time as president of the ministerial council, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So among other things he speaks up here, doesn't he, to report the -- quite fully the decision that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina had adopted the previous day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if we just go back about a page into the contribution of Professor Koljevic, this will be two or three paragraphs after the margin note 5 appears on your document, so it probably is going to be very near to the top of page 14 on your copy, Mr. Krajisnik, and about halfway down page 8 in the English, a paragraph beginning, "One day historians may be able to draw some interesting conclusions from yesterday's meeting of the Presidency but I must tell you one thing. The joint position of Nikola Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic in relation to the second item on the agenda was not included in the statement of the Presidency, not a single sentence was included, not even one sentence that I insisted be included, so I would like to inform you and the Yugoslav public about our position in relation to the second item on the agenda at yesterday's meeting, that is our response to the European office -- offer for independence. This is the text of our position, that we submitted to the Presidency yesterday, 'We are opposed to Bosnia and Herzegovina submitting an application for independence with the European Community in accordance with the right to self determination under the declaration on the guidelines for recognition of new states and many other international treaties, the Serbian people exercising that right is vehemently opposed to the request in question and holds that it has the right to remain within Yugoslavia.'" Mr. Krajisnik, was the concern expressed here by Professor Koljevic that his and Mrs. Plavsic's position should be known, was that to yours and Mr. Ostojic's expressed wish that there should be as wide television coverage as possible?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. But there is something I would like to add. This is a document -- just like the government passed a decision, the Presidency passed a decision too. But in that decision for Bosnia-Herzegovina to apply for independence, there was an annex as well, the statement made by Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic. And that was supposed possible made public because they were opposed to it. They had a different view. And that was not the case. And now he is saying since the television crews are there, I want the public to know what was dropped from this press release. Now I'm talking on behalf of the late Mr. Koljevic. That is what he and Mrs. Plavsic stated in terms of their own views, and he wanted it to be made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Going back to Mr. Simovic's contribution, if you would find the margin note 7 on your copy, Mr. Krajisnik, that would be on page 19, about a third of the way down, and on the English it's in the middle of page 10.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll go just above 7, paragraph beginning, "We expressed our position in relation to this decision in a separate statement entitled, 'Black Friday for Bosnia and Herzegovina.'" As far as I'm aware, it has not been published in the media so, please, let me read it out. In response -- quotes in response to today's --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the interpreters have trouble finding the reference and they should read this out. So could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It's on page 19 of the B/C/S. I think it's actual will he at the very foot of page 18 probably. "Nase," is that a word that makes sense, as I say it, "Nase stavove"? Is that the right paragraph? In English, "We expressed our position." Does that help?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we found it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found it and I think they have too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They have, Mr. Krajisnik. "We expressed our position in relation to this position in a separate statement entitled, black Friday for Bosnia and Herzegovina. As far as I am aware it has not been published in the media so please let me read it out. Quotes, in response to today's session of the government of BiH which adopted by a majority vote the decision to send a request to the EC to recognise the sovereignty, autonomy and independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the members of the government of BiH representing the Serbian people consider this act as a flagrant violation of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, SRBiH, and the statute of the government of SRBiH. For the Serbian people in BiH who have expressed their will to live in Yugoslavia, the EC declaration on the possibility of recognition of Yugoslav republics is completely irrelevant, which makes the decision of the government of BiH meaningless. The Serbian people in BiH will never, under any circumstances, accept to be subordinated to anybody and especially will not accept the status of a minority in their own state, a state they will defend and promote using all means and in a manner that they have always been doing. Therefore, Serbian people are defending their existing right and its unity and all they want is peaceful coexistence with other peoples who want the same. The Serbian people in Bosnia, together with other sections of the Serbian people in Yugoslavia will never accept the humiliation of having their state created and recognised by others and especially its destruction by a stroke of pen at a conference table by those who have not created it. Serbian people accept only the principles of the Charter of the UN and the CSCE that embody truth and justice and, in particular, the right of people to self-determination." And he says, "That was our statement." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Simovic says in the course of that statement, says, in the course of it, as far as the Serbian people are concerned, all they want is peaceful coexistence with other peoples who want the same. At that point, was the statement in line with your own position, with the SDS position at this time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: However, is -- would it have been a correct understanding of what Mr. Simovic was saying there, that if coexistence with other peoples could not be achieved peacefully, then the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina would fight? And when I say "fight", I mean fight a war.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I mean, I didn't notice it here, but probably Mr. Simovic said this because he felt revolted because he is a very refined intellectual, a member of the Academy of Sciences and Arts, and he's even a member of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it doesn't sound like him but it was probably an expression of revolt. If we can't do it peacefully we are going to wage war. I didn't really notice while you were reading it out but if he said it, he's saying we are proposing to resolve it by peaceful means now, now what is the opposite of peace? It is war. So it is something that no one wanted. So perhaps it was just for propaganda purposes, a bit of propaganda, but we wanted to find a solution at all costs, a peaceful solution, for several reasons. First of all, war would not help anyone achieve anything, and also, we were a third of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in every war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs were major victims of any war. We were afraid of war. And the other two peoples were too. I have to be fair about that. No one wanted war. People were all afraid of war, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go on to number 8 in the margin, which is at page 23 of your copy, your version, Mr. Krajisnik, and page 12 of the English, it's near the top of the page in each case, do you see, about -- a paragraph that begins, "During the election campaign, not a single party ..."?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
